grounded_in: Publicly documented Google Cloud pricing model concepts (on-demand vs. committed-use/sustained-use discounts, Spot VM pricing, disk pricing tiers, BigQuery on-demand vs. flat-rate/editions, Cloud Run scaling billing) and Google Cloud Recommender / Active Assist insight categories. Prices change; this checklist intentionally never hardcodes a $/unit figure -- see references/gcp_pricing_and_quotas.md and re-verify current rates against the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator before quoting a number to a user.
note: Each entry is the canonical metadata for one waste pattern. scripts/audit_gcp_costs.py loads this file at runtime and only implements a check() function for entries where automated is true. `waste_fraction` is the fraction of a resource's own monthly_cost_usd (if the inventory input supplies one) treated as recoverable if the recommendation is followed -- it is a documented estimate, not a live pricing lookup, and the script always labels it as such.

resource_categories.compute_instances: google_compute_instance equivalents: name, zone, machine_type, status, cpu_utilization_pct_p95 (optional), is_preemptible_or_spot, labels, monthly_cost_usd (optional)
resource_categories.persistent_disks: google_compute_disk equivalents: name, zone, size_gb, type, attached_instances (list, empty = unattached), last_attached_days_ago (optional), monthly_cost_usd (optional)
resource_categories.static_ips: google_compute_address equivalents: name, region, status (RESERVED|IN_USE), users (list), monthly_cost_usd (optional)
resource_categories.bigquery_reservations: BigQuery reservation equivalents: name, slots, avg_utilization_pct (trailing-30-day average), monthly_cost_usd (optional)
resource_categories.bigquery_datasets: BigQuery dataset equivalents: dataset_id, active_storage_gb, long_term_storage_gb, default_table_expiration_days (0/null = unset), monthly_cost_usd (optional)
resource_categories.cloud_run_services: Cloud Run service equivalents: name, region, min_instances, max_instances, cpu, concurrency, avg_requests_per_min (optional), monthly_cost_usd (optional)

controls.title: Running instance with sustained near-zero CPU utilization
controls.rationale: An instance running 24/7 at p95 CPU utilization under the idle threshold is very likely a forgotten dev/test box or an over-provisioned service that could be stopped, scheduled, or replaced with a smaller machine type -- Compute Engine bills for uptime regardless of whether the workload is doing anything.
controls.recommendation: If the workload is not needed continuously: stop it and use an instance schedule (Cloud Scheduler + start/stop, or the built-in schedule feature) instead of running it 24/7. If it must run continuously but rarely uses CPU: run `gcloud recommender recommendations list --recommender=google.compute.instance.MachineTypeRecommender` for a data-driven rightsizing suggestion rather than guessing a smaller machine type.

controls.title: Fault-tolerant-labeled workload not using Spot/Preemptible VMs
controls.rationale: Spot VMs run at a large discount off on-demand pricing (see references/gcp_pricing_and_quotas.md for current mechanics) in exchange for possible preemption. A workload the owner has already labeled as batch/fault-tolerant is a strong signal it can tolerate that tradeoff and is very likely leaving savings on the table by running on-demand.
controls.recommendation: Confirm the workload is genuinely restartable (checkpointing, a job queue, a managed instance group that reschedules), then migrate to Spot VMs (google_compute_instance.scheduling.provisioning_model = "SPOT" or a Spot-backed MIG). Never apply this to anything stateful or latency-sensitive without an explicit owner sign-off -- preemption is real, not theoretical.

controls.title: Persistent disk not attached to any instance
controls.rationale: An unattached persistent disk provides zero compute value while billing for its full provisioned size every month -- these accumulate silently after instance deletions/migrations when the disk's `auto_delete` was left false, or the disk was intentionally detached and never cleaned up.
controls.recommendation: If the data is still needed: snapshot it (google_compute_snapshot) for cold storage at a fraction of the disk cost, then delete the disk. If the data is not needed: delete it directly. Never delete without a snapshot unless the disk is confirmed scratch/ephemeral data.

controls.title: pd-ssd disk with no documented high-IOPS requirement
controls.rationale: pd-ssd costs meaningfully more per GB than pd-balanced, which covers the IOPS/throughput needs of most general-purpose workloads. Defaulting to pd-ssd 'to be safe' is a common source of avoidable disk spend.
controls.recommendation: This is advisory, not a confirmed finding -- verify the workload's actual IOPS/throughput requirement (databases with heavy random write load may genuinely need pd-ssd or pd-extreme) before downgrading. If unverified, propose pd-balanced as the default going forward for new disks rather than silently migrating existing ones.

controls.title: Reserved static external IP not attached to any resource
controls.rationale: Google Cloud charges for a static external IP address specifically while it is reserved but NOT in use (attached, in-use static IPs are not charged the idle rate) -- an unattached reservation is pure waste with no offsetting benefit.
controls.recommendation: Release the static IP if it is no longer needed, or attach it to the resource it was reserved for. Confirm it isn't referenced by an external DNS record or firewall rule allow-list before releasing.

controls.title: BigQuery flat-rate/editions slot reservation is significantly under-utilized
controls.rationale: A flat-rate or Editions slot commitment bills for the committed capacity regardless of how much of it is actually used. Sustained low utilization means on-demand pricing (billed per TB scanned) or a smaller commitment would likely be cheaper for the same workload.
controls.recommendation: Compare the trailing-30-day average utilization against the commitment cost using BigQuery's own reservation utilization charts (or `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS` slot usage). If sustained under ~30% utilization, consider reducing the commitment size, switching to autoscaling reservations, or moving the workload to on-demand pricing.

controls.title: Large dataset has no default table/partition expiration set
controls.rationale: Without `default_table_expiration_ms` (or per-partition expiration), tables accumulate indefinitely. Active storage costs more than long-term storage (data untouched for 90+ days), but data nobody ever queries again should usually be exported/deleted rather than paying long-term storage rates forever.
controls.recommendation: Set a `default_table_expiration_ms` at the dataset level (or `time_partitioning.expiration_ms` per table) sized to the team's actual retention need, especially for staging/scratch/log datasets. Confirm no compliance/audit requirement mandates longer retention before applying an expiration.

controls.title: Cloud Run service holds warm min_instances with low observed traffic
controls.rationale: `min_instances > 0` bills for that many always-on instances regardless of request volume, trading cold-start latency for a continuous baseline cost. A service with low average request volume is very likely over-paying for warm capacity it rarely needs.
controls.recommendation: Reduce `min_instances` toward 0 (accepting occasional cold starts) unless the service has a documented latency SLA that requires warm instances; if partial warmth is needed, size `min_instances` to the p50 concurrent request count instead of a round number picked without traffic data.

controls.title: Multi-vCPU Cloud Run service configured with concurrency = 1
controls.rationale: Cloud Run bills per-instance for the CPU/memory allocated to it. `concurrency = 1` on a 2+ vCPU instance means only one request is ever served per allocated vCPU pair at a time -- the extra vCPU capacity is provisioned but structurally unable to be used unless the request handler is itself multi-threaded.
controls.recommendation: Either raise `concurrency` so multiple requests share the provisioned CPU (if the handler is thread-/async-safe), or reduce `cpu` to match the single-request workload if concurrency must stay at 1.

controls.title: Steady-state on-demand compute spend not covered by a Committed Use Discount
controls.rationale: Committed Use Discounts (1- or 3-year, spend-based or resource-based) discount steady-state compute spend that's already known to be stable -- but committing requires 6-12 months of stable historical usage trend to size safely, which a point-in-time inventory snapshot cannot show on its own.
controls.recommendation: Pull the trailing 6-12 month usage trend from Cloud Billing reports or `gcloud recommender recommendations list --recommender=google.compute.commitment.UsageCommitmentRecommender` (which is already trend-aware) rather than committing off a single inventory snapshot. Verify manually.

controls.title: Custom images and disk snapshots retained with no lifecycle/retention policy
controls.rationale: Snapshots and custom images are cheap individually but accumulate indefinitely without a retention policy, and a normalized point-in-time inventory of disks does not typically enumerate every historical snapshot/image or its age -- that requires a separate `gcloud compute snapshots list` / `gcloud compute images list` pass this checklist does not model.
controls.recommendation: Set a Snapshot Schedule with a retention policy (`google_compute_resource_policy` snapshot schedule) instead of ad hoc manual snapshots, and audit `gcloud compute snapshots list --format='table(name,diskSizeGb,creationTimestamp)'` for old entries with no matching active disk. Verify manually.
